idiom_name: NestJS CanActivate guard registered globally (APP_GUARD) with a deny-unless-marked default; exhaustive typed decisions
implementation_notes: The guard seam is framework-provided (an `@Injectable()` class implementing `CanActivate`, with `ExecutionContext` and `Reflector` metadata; returning false makes Nest throw `ForbiddenException`), but the documented example is fail-open: the roles guard returns true when a handler carries no roles metadata ('if (!roles) { return true; }'). The pattern's realization therefore inverts that branch - no metadata means deny, and public routes carry an explicit marker decorator - and registers the guard once with the `APP_GUARD` provider so every controller, present and future, inherits the decision (the docs note the guard is global regardless of which module registers it, and that `useGlobalGuards` cannot inject dependencies). TypeScript's half is the decision type: model it as a discriminated union and switch exhaustively so a new case cannot fall into a permissive branch - remembering that types are erased and the runtime check is the enforcement.
pitfalls: The NestJS docs' own `RolesGuard` returns `true` when no `@Roles()` metadata is present; copying it leaves every unannotated handler public. Invert the branch so absence of metadata denies, and mark public routes explicitly.

Guards are per-controller/per-method unless registered globally; global registration must use the `APP_GUARD` provider (the docs note `useGlobalGuards` cannot inject dependencies), and hybrid apps do not get guards for gateways and microservices from it by default.

`Reflector.get` returns `undefined` both for 'no metadata' and 'metadata explicitly undefined', and `getAllAndOverride` silently lets a class-level grant override a narrower method-level decision - resolve precedence deliberately.

Types are erased at runtime: a `Policy` interface promising a `Decision` can be satisfied by a stub (`{ allowed: true }`) or an `as any` cast; the runtime decision is the enforcement point, so test unknown subjects and actions and keep the decision object unforgeable.

Decorator metadata depends on `emitDecoratorMetadata`/`experimentalDecorators`: if the build stops emitting it, a deny-when-unmarked guard fails closed (safe) while an allow-when-unmarked design would silently open everything - one more reason to keep the default on the deny side.
